title: North Star Summit
subtitle: Data science with Mr. Hayward
status: Tentative schedule. Dates and time await school confirmation.

modules.title: Meet Mr. Hayward. What is data science?
modules.focus: Start with the slides, meet your classmates, and tell us what you want to learn.
modules.objective: Describe data science in your own words and set a personal learning goal.
questions: Why are you taking this course?
What would you like to be able to do by April?
What is one question you would like to answer with data?
What experience do you have with spreadsheets or coding?
modules.deliverable: Your introduction and learning goals in the welcome Form.
modules.practice: Look through the opening slides. Share your goals in the Form so Mr. Hayward and your teachers can get to know you.
modules.check: Your answers sound like you. There is no right background or perfect goal.
modules.source: S16; welcome goals Form created September 28, 2026

modules.title: Explore Mr. Hayward’s weight in Sheets
modules.focus: Open your own student Sheet. It contains the data and questions, with blank spaces for your formulas and explanations.
modules.objective: Use COUNT, MEDIAN, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and a conditional average to answer questions reproducibly.
questions: How many observations are in the data?
What is the median weight?
What is the average weight?
What is the lowest weight?
What is the highest weight?
What is the average weight on weekends?
Explain one formula and the range it uses.
modules.deliverable: Six spreadsheet results, formulas and your explanation. Submit your answers and Sheet link in the assignment Form.
modules.practice: Your teachers will give you a personal copy of the blank student Sheet. Use the Data tab to answer the six questions in My work. Send your first questions by November 5, bring them to the November 12 workshop, submit a first attempt by November 18, and finish by December 3. Try either or both optional bonuses in November.
modules.check: Your formulas refer to the Data tab. Your teachers can open your personal Sheet.

bonuses.title: Bonus 1 · Spot a weight-gain streak
bonuses.text: Define a streak: consecutive recorded observations or consecutive calendar days? Decide what happens when a day is missing or the weight stays equal. Then try finding the longest streak. This optional extension adapts the historical streak challenge.

bonuses.title: Bonus 2 · Try VLOOKUP
bonuses.text: Build a small lookup table with one row for each weekday and its mean weight. Use VLOOKUP with an exact match (FALSE) to return the mean for a chosen weekday. Check it against a filtered average.

checkpoints.label: Submit your goals and first spreadsheet questions
Spreadsheet check-in and optional bonus workshop
Mr. Hayward returns feedback on your first attempt
Send any remaining spreadsheet or bonus questions
Submit final Sheet and any optional bonuses

modules.title: From formulas to Python
modules.focus: Solve the same questions in code.
modules.objective: Use pandas methods and Boolean filtering; distinguish a computed result from a typed answer.
questions: What is the lowest weight?
What is the highest weight?
What is max minus min, rounded using code?
What is the earliest date?
What is the latest date?
What is the latest date marked as a holiday?
Explain one Boolean filter in your code.
modules.deliverable: Executed Python answers to six questions, with one sentence explaining a filter. Paste the code you used and its result into the assignment Form, as well as your notebook link.
modules.practice: Work through A02 in your notebook. Compare Python results with your spreadsheet. Save the outputs.
modules.check: Restart and run all cells. Explain ==, a Boolean, and one method used.

modules.title: Ask a better data question
modules.focus: Explore what “tends to” means before choosing a statistic.
modules.objective: Filter a dataframe and distinguish a minimum observation from a typical value.
questions: On what day of the week does Mr. Hayward tend to weigh the least?
Which statistic answers that question, and why?
modules.deliverable: A draft table for all seven weekdays and a justified choice of statistic. Paste the code you used and its result into the assignment Form, as well as your notebook link.
modules.practice: Read the weekday example. Produce a count and mean for each weekday; try min and max too.
modules.check: Explain why the weekday with the lowest minimum need not have the lowest mean.

modules.title: Write a clear letter to your teacher
modules.focus: Turn your weekday analysis into an email a busy colleague can understand.
modules.objective: Write a concise finding, evidence, limitation and next question.
questions: What does the seven-day comparison show?
What is a plausible hypothesis, and what additional data would test it?
modules.deliverable: A 150–250 word work-style email or letter to your teacher: subject, greeting, finding, evidence, limitation and next question. Paste the complete letter into the Form and keep a copy in your notebook.
modules.practice: Write an email to Mr. Hayward explaining which weekday tends to have the lowest weight. Use the same numbers as your analysis. Paste the draft into the assignment Form; you do not need to send an email.
modules.check: Lead with the finding. Match the numbers to your notebook and label hypotheses as hypotheses.

modules.title: See the distribution
modules.focus: Make a weekend histogram and explain the shape you see.
modules.objective: Create a labeled histogram and compare groups using consistent bins and sample counts.
questions: What does the weekend weight distribution look like?
What changes when you adjust the bins?
How does it compare with weekdays, given different sample sizes?
modules.deliverable: A labeled weekend histogram and a short comparison with weekdays in the notebook. Paste the code you used and its result into the assignment Form, as well as your notebook link.
modules.practice: Make the weekend chart, use common bins for comparison, and report the observation count in each group.
modules.check: Chart title and axes identify the subset and units. Do not interpret fewer observations as lower weight.

modules.title: Put time back into the story
modules.focus: Make a time-series chart. See what a single average leaves out.
modules.objective: Parse and sort dates, plot a time series, and explain the limits of a summary statistic.
questions: What is the overall average weight?
Why might giving only that average be misleading?
What pattern is visible when the observations are ordered by time?
modules.deliverable: A dated time-series chart, computed overall mean, and an explanation linked to code. Paste the code you used and its result into the assignment Form, as well as your notebook link.
modules.practice: After the histogram, make a chart with real dates on the horizontal axis. Compare what it shows with the single overall mean.
modules.check: Date axis reflects real dates. Written claims name the relevant time period and avoid unsupported causes.

modules.title: Redo your work with Gemini. Check its answers.
modules.focus: Revisit a question you already solved. Use AI to help, then judge the result yourself.
modules.objective: Use AI to produce a useful data artifact and verify its claims against reproducible work.
questions: Which spreadsheet question and Python or chart task did you ask Gemini to redo?
What exact prompts did you use, and what did Gemini produce?
Which parts do you agree with, and what evidence supports them?
Which parts are wrong, uncertain or incomplete, and how did you correct them?
What are the pros and cons of using Gemini for this work? What should still be checked by a person?
modules.deliverable: An AI-assisted Google Doc or Sheet (or a notebook section), your prompt, two independent checks and a short critique.
modules.practice: After completing the spreadsheet and Python work, ask school-approved Gemini to redo at least one spreadsheet question and one Python or chart task. Give it only Mr. Hayward’s public dataset. Save the prompts, response and a useful Doc, Sheet or notebook artifact. Compare its results with your own work and independently check two numerical claims. Explain what was faster, what you agree or disagree with, and the pros and cons of relying on it. If Gemini is unavailable, ask your teacher for a response to evaluate. Pause during assessments and spring break.
modules.check: Show the original AI output and your corrections. Do not assume AI opened the URL: ask what rows and columns it actually read. Use only the public teaching dataset.
modules.source: New 2026–27 module requested by George; tool availability subject to school account settings

modules.title: Show us what you learned
modules.focus: Present your best analysis and explain how you know it is right.
modules.objective: Present an evidence-based finding, explain a code choice and reflect on AI assistance.
questions: What is your main finding and the evidence for it?
What did AI help with, and what did you have to check or change?
What three tips would you give a new student?
How did your work connect to the goal you set at the start?
modules.deliverable: A four-slide presentation, final notebook and short reflection. Paste your Slides link and reflection in the Form. Present in mid-April.
modules.practice: Prepare four slides: your question; a chart with evidence and a code excerpt; Gemini’s help, mistakes and your independent checks; and three tips for future students. Submit a draft by April 8, use feedback by April 12, and present on April 15. Your teachers will share a clean presentation example.
modules.check: You can explain your chart, one code choice, a limitation, and one AI check without simply reading generated text.

links.geminiPrompt: For this conversation, please be my data analysis helper. Work only with Mr. Hayward's public weight data. It is on this page as CSV text: https://www.haywarddatascience.com/summit2026_2027/data.html (if I attached mr_hayward_weight.csv, use that file instead). It has one row per day and five columns: date, weight (in pounds), day_of_week, is_weekend and is_holiday. Before anything else, tell me how many rows and columns you read and the first and last date, so I can check you really read all of it. Whenever you give me a number, show the formula or Python code you used so I can check it myself. If you cannot read the data or are not sure, say so instead of guessing. Then wait for my first question.

submissionNote: Each lesson has its own Google Form. Type your answers and paste the link to your work. The Form receipt is your submission confirmation.
